elements.note: Italic, set across the full measure and turned over two lines; `COMMUNION` is in small capitals and is broken `COMMU-` / `NION` at the turn. The book gives no Communion antiphon text here, only this cross-reference.

translations.text: Then he returns to the Book, and reads the COMMUNION, which may be seen in its proper place.

elements.name: Dominus vobiscum
elements.note: Three lines set as one block in both columns; only the response carries `R.`, the priest's parts being unmarked. `Oremus.` / `Let us pray.` is centred on its own line within the same block.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: The Lord be with you. R. And with thy spirit. Let us pray.
Dominus vobiscum. R. Et cum spiritu tuo. Oremus.

elements.note: Set across the full measure with roman and italic alternating word by word: the named seasons and feasts are roman, the connective matter italic. `POSTCOMMUNION` in small capitals. Ends without punctuation, running straight into the heading of the next block.

translations.text: From Candlemas-day till Passion Sunday, and from the III. Sunday after Pentecost until Advent, (except on Doubles and within Octaves) after the proper POSTCOMMUNION, the following is the

elements.note: Set across the full measure with NO facing Latin column; `latin_incipit` is therefore empty, but the book supplies its own Latin cue as the parenthesis `(Mundet.)`, which is italic. `II. POSTCOM.` is roman full capitals and is part of the printed paragraph, so it is transcribed here.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: II. POSTCOM. (Mundet.) May the oblation of this divine sacrament, we beseech thee, O Lord, both cleanse and defend us; and by the intercession of the blessed Mary the Virgin Mother of God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of blessed N. and of all the saints, free us from all sin, and deliver us from all adversity.

elements.note: Set across the full measure, roman and italic alternating as in row 6. `COMM.` in small capitals, `SALVE` in full capitals. The asterisk after `P. COMM.` is printed on the page but has NO answering footnote anywhere on xliii, which is blank below this point but for the following rubric.

translations.text: From Low Sunday, exclusively, till the Ascension, instead of the foregoing, is said the P. COMM. * Sumptis, &c. as in the Votive Mass SALVE for the B. V. M. p. 509.

elements.note: Set across the full measure in ROMAN, not italic, unlike every other rubric in this range; it is the last thing printed on xliii and its sentence is completed by the heading at the head of xliv.

translations.text: After the Postcommunion, is added the following

elements.note: Centred at the head of xliv across the full measure. `PRAYER.` roman full capitals, `(Et famulos.)` italic; the parenthesis is the book's own Latin cue for a prayer it prints in English only.

translations.text: PRAYER. (Et famulos.)

elements.note: Two-line drop D, transcribed as an ordinary capital; `EFEND` is in full capitals beside it. Set across the full measure with NO facing Latin column. The book prints a blank line after `our Bishop,` and then a blank space of about an inch within the line, between `people` and `committed`; inspected at 1000 dpi and there is no ink there at all, so the gap is the book's own setting, not scan loss.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: DEFEND also, O Lord, from all adversity, thy servant N. our Pope, N. our Bishop, together with the people committed to his care: grant peace in our days, and banish all wickedness from thy Church: thro', &c.

elements.name: Dominus vobiscum
elements.note: The book sets the greeting and the dismissal as ONE block with no break: Latin `Dominus vobiscum. / R. Et cum spiritu tuo. / Ite missa est (vel) Benedicamus Domino. / R. Deo gratias.` The English renders `Ite missa est` as `Go, you are dismissed,` and gives the alternative in the same sentence as `(or) let us bless the Lord.` No rubric governs the choice between them.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: The Lord be with you. R. And with thy spirit. Go, you are dismissed, (or) let us bless the Lord. R. Thanks be to God.
Dominus vobiscum. R. Et cum spiritu tuo. Ite missa est (vel) Benedicamus Domino. R. Deo gratias.

elements.note: Italic, centred across the full measure.

translations.text: In Masses for the Dead.

elements.name: Requiescant in pace
elements.note: Both columns print `P.` and `R.`, unlike the two preceding dialogues. `Amen.` is italic in both columns. Scan damage: `in` of `rest in peace` prints as `iu`, the n having lost its right stem at the column edge; read against the facing Latin `Requiescant in pace`.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: P. May they rest in peace. R. Amen.
P. Requiescant in pace. R. Amen.

elements.note: Italic, centred across the full measure. It ends with NO terminal comma, where every other `he says` rubric in this range takes one; checked at 1000 dpi.

translations.text: Bowing before the Altar, the Priest says

elements.name: Placeat tibi sancta Trinitas
elements.note: The English column ends on the bare word `Thro'` with no full stop and no `&c.`, where the facing Latin sets the conclusion out in full, `Per Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.` Checked at 1000 dpi: nothing follows `Thro'`, and it is not a case of lost ink. `tho'` and `thro'` are the book's spellings.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: Let the performance of my homage be pleasing to thee, O holy Trinity; and grant that the sacrifice which I, tho' unworthy, have offered up in the sight of thy Majesty, may be acceptable to thee, and thro' thy mercy be a propitiation for me, and all those for whom it has been offered. Thro'

Placeat tibi sancta Trinitas, obsequium servitutis meæ; et præsta, ut sacrificium quod oculis tuæ Majestatis indignus obtuli, tibi sit acceptabile, mihique, et omnibus pro quibus illud obtuli, sit te miserante, propitiabile. Per Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.

elements.note: Italic, set across the full measure and turned over two lines.

translations.text: Turning himself towards the People, he gives them his Blessing, saying,

elements.note: `kind` is `form` as the closest of the five permitted values; it is the blessing formula, not an oration. Set across the full measure in English ONLY: there is no Latin `Benedicat vos omnipotens Deus`, and the single cross sign the Latin rite prescribes is printed in NEITHER column, no cross glyph appearing anywhere on this opening. `Amen.` is italic.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: May Almighty God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, bless you. Amen.

elements.name: Dominus vobiscum
elements.note: Runs over the page break at xliv/xlv. The Latin opens `P. Dominus vobiscum.` and continues `P. Initium sancti Evangelii, secundum Joannem. R. Gloria tibi, Domine.` This greeting is rendered `Our Lord be with you`, against `The Lord be with you` at rows 5 and 12 of the same range. The book prints no rubric for signing the book, the forehead, the lips or the breast.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: P. Our Lord be with you. R. And with thy spirit. P. The beginning of the Gospel according to St. John. R. Glory be to thee, O Lord.
P. Dominus vobiscum. R. Et cum spiritu tuo. P. Initium sancti Evangelii, secundum Joannem. R. Gloria tibi, Domine.

elements.name: In principio erat Verbum
elements.note: `kind` is `prayer` as the closest of the five permitted values; this is a Gospel lection, not an oration. Two-line drop I in both columns, transcribed as an ordinary capital, with `N` in full capitals beside it. The book divides the last Gospel into three paragraphs which the two columns keep aligned, and this is the first. Scan damage: `the` in `in the beginning` prints as `thc` and `ning` in `beginning with God` prints as `nmg`, both broken types rather than margin loss; read against the facing Latin `hoc erat in principio apud Deum`.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: IN the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: the same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him, and without him was made nothing that was made; in him was life, and the life was the light of men: and the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

IN principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum: et Deus erat Verbum: hoc erat in principio apud Deum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est: in ipso vita erat, et vita erat lux hominum: et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt.

elements.name: Fuit homo missus a Deo
elements.note: Second of the three paragraphs of the last Gospel; both columns break here. `through` is set out in full, where the same book abbreviates to `thro'` elsewhere on this opening.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. This man came for a witness, to give testimony of the light, that all men might believe through him. He was not the light, but was to give testimony of the light. That was the true light which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world.

Fuit homo missus a Deo, cui nomen erat Joannes. Hic venit in testimonium, ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine, ut omnes crederent per illum. Non erat ille lux; sed ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine. Erat lux vera quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum.

elements.name: In mundo erat, et mundus
elements.note: Runs over the page break at xlv/xlvi. `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH` is in small capitals, the run beginning after the roman `And` and ending at `FLESH`, the following comma and `and dwelt` returning to roman; the facing Latin sets `VERBUM CARO FACTUM EST` in the same small capitals, beginning after the roman `Et`. NO rubric about genuflecting is printed at this point in either column, nor anywhere in the last Gospel; the small capitals are the only mark the book makes of the place. Scan damage: `be` in `power to be made` has lost the bowl of its b; read against the facing Latin `dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri`.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.text: He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not. He came unto his own, and his own received him not. But as many as received him, to them he gave power to be made the sons of God: to them that believe in his name, who are born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God: And THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH, and dwelt among us; and we saw his glory, as it were the glory of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.

In mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit. In propria venit, et sui eum non receperunt. Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri: his qui credunt in nomine ejus, qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt: Et VERBUM CARO FACTUM EST, et habitavit in nobis; et vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi unigeniti a Patre, plenum gratiæ et veritatis.

elements.name: Deo gratias
elements.note: The last thing printed above the rule that closes the Ordinary. Set as its own block, indented, after a blank line; the Latin column prints `R. Deo gratias.` opposite. Immediately below it runs a thick-and-thin double rule across the full measure, and below that rule xlvi is entirely blank to the foot of the page.
elements.speaker: server

translations.text: R. Thanks be to God.
R. Deo gratias.

slots_derived_from: Where each proper of the day stands inside this frame is read from the 1962 typical edition itself - the Ritus servandus in celebratione Missae and the Ordo Missae - and not from the 1861 witness whose words the elements carry. Each slot names the paragraph of the Ritus servandus that states the place; where the position of a seasonal chant is stated instead by a rubric of the Proprium de Tempore, the slot names that rubric beside it, by its marginal number and printed page. The two books agree on the order of these nine positions, which is why the anchors below are 1861 elements and the loci are 1962 rubrics; where they did not agree, no slot would be declared.
